items.title: 'They will kill you too': Sonia Gandhi's turbulent journey in Indian politics
items.summary: Sonia Gandhi's memoir revisits love, loss and political inheritance, offering a deeply personal defence of her family and its legacy.
items.content:
On the morning of 31 October 1984, Sonia Gandhi was a young wife and mother, living in the prime minister's residence in Delhi. She was about to take a bath when she heard shots ring out in the garden.

Her mother-in-law, Indira Gandhi, India's prime minister, had just left for her office in an adjoining building. Moments later, she would be assassinated by two of her Sikh bodyguards, in retaliation for the Indian army's storming of the Golden Temple in Amritsar, Sikhism's holiest shrine, earlier that year.

The sound was like firecrackers, but "different". The children's nanny came pounding on the bathroom door, hysterical, pointing towards the garden.

Sonia ran towards the path. A white Ambassador car was moving slowly towards her. Inside, Indira lay covered in blood, her sari stained, her eyes open, her face wearing what Sonia remembered as a look of surprise.

"Mummy, Mummy," she tried to say. No words came. At the hospital, she waited for hours before a doctor's shake of the head told her what she feared.

The ordeal did not end there. Rajiv Gandhi, her husband and the elder son of Indira Gandhi, summoned from a rally in West Bengal, arrived to tell her that party leaders wanted him to become prime minister.

Sonia's response was fury and terror. "They will kill you; they will kill you, too!" she pleaded. Rajiv replied: "They will kill me anyway." That evening, as Indira's body lay at home, Rajiv was sworn in.

It is one of the most searing passages in Belonging: A Journey of Love, Sonia Gandhi's new memoir: private devastation unfolding alongside the pressures of public life.

The woman who had largely stayed away from politics was now married to India's prime minister, and would eventually find herself at the head of the Congress party, leading it through two general election victories and becoming one of the country's most consequential political figures.

The passage also foreshadows another devastating loss. In 1991, Rajiv himself was assassinated.

At 19, a young woman from a small Italian town, she had met Rajiv, an Indian student, in England. Their relationship took her into a new country and family, and a close bond with Indira followed. India became home through her husband and her mother-in-law.

After Rajiv's killing, even the public appearances required by the memorial trusts she headed became an ordeal. Before speeches, she feared tears would overwhelm her.

When the Dalai Lama asked whether she felt vengeful towards her husband's killers, she answered, "No, I don't," and burst into sobs. Slowly, she writes, Rajiv became "a presence within me rather than a piercing absence".

But grief returned at family milestones. At her son Rahul's Cambridge graduation in 1995, she and her children were overcome by the thought of how proud Rajiv would have been.

Politics, meanwhile, was closing in. The Congress party, the political vehicle of her husband's family for generations, was losing cohesion and electoral ground. Senior leaders were defecting, and the calls for Sonia to step in were growing louder.

She initially refused. She writes she had seen politics through Rajiv: its achievements, but also its "ambition and greed, hypocrisy and treachery". "I'd always disliked politics," she writes. It had taken first her mother-in-law, then "the love of my life, my children's father".

Yet the party's decline began to feel personal. Walking past photographs of Indira and Rajiv, she was seized by "a mixture of pain and guilt". She feared that the forces they had fought to "protect India's pluralistic ethos" were gaining ground: a rising Hindu nationalism that, in her view, threatened the "secular and pluralistic vision" of India they had sought to defend.

Congress leaders argued that without her, the party could splinter, leaving little to resist communal politics. The family name, she believed, carried an appeal beyond religion, caste, language and region. This, she says, was "the most compelling argument".

Her doubts were also about her own credentials. How could an outsider occupy a position held by two formidable figures? At home, Rahul and Priyanka feared losing their mother as they had lost their grandmother and father. Before a New Year holiday, they extracted a promise: "Don't you do anything crazy while we're away."

The "answer", she says, came through the Bhagavad Gita . Though not religious in adult life, Sonia arranged private lessons with a Sanskrit scholar in January 1997. They read the text verse by verse. She writes that its central message – to perform one's dharma, or duty, without attachment to the fruits of one's actions – eventually resolved her inner conflict.

"I had the answer to my own doubts and questions. I had to step out and go where my duty called. And I did."

The memoir's most dramatic political scene, however, comes seven years later, after Congress's 2004 election victory . Sonia had led the party's campaign.

Sonia goes with Manmohan Sing h to meet India's president at the presidential palace in Delhi and formally stake the Congress-led alliance's claim to form a government. Everyone assumes she will become prime minister. She says nothing.

At home, she tells a senior aide she intends to refuse. Party workers gather at the gates; senior colleagues demand a meeting.

"You fought the election, you led us," says one. "People believed in you. How can you let them down like this? Our workers will revolt. You think they'll accept another leader?"

Alliance leaders arrive to persuade her. They surround her, she recalls, and one insists: "We will not take no for an answer." Overwhelmed, she murmurs " Theek hai " - all right. They take it as consent and begin congratulating her.

Her children are appalled, she writes. Rahul storms in: "You said yes?" Her daughter Priyanka urges her not to be forced into a decision.

Sonia writes she spends a long night arguing with herself, friends and family. The risk is not merely personal. She believes the main opposition Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) would continue to exploit her foreign birth and that accepting office would allow the controversy to "create havoc" and hurt the country. By morning she is clear. " I've made up my mind . I'm going to stick to my stand," she tells Rahul.

She chooses Singh, a trained economist and a party member, instead, describing him as a man "above reproach", with a "deep and consummate understanding of governance".

The book is at its most revealing when it turns from family memory to the India she believes has been lost.

Sonia says that when she entered public life there was "a certain decency and decorum in parliamentary politics".

Political attacks and harsh words were not new, but she sees a sharper appetite among those in power "to belittle and torment those who differ from them, to intimidate those they perceive as opponents". It is, she says, part of a wider international drift towards "a heartlessness that accompanies authoritarian regimes".

Her portrait of prime minister Narendra Modi of the Hindu nationalist BJP is unusually direct.

The two have had "practically no real contact", she writes, beyond formal greetings at parliamentary gatherings and occasional exchanges - " Theek hain, aap ?" ("Are you all right?") - when she returned from hospital. "He tends to look away," she says, "avoiding eye contact."

Modi's idea of India, she writes, was shaped by the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh (RSS) and "affirmed a fundamentalism in which his faith and culture superseded all others". His is an India of "hierarchy, order, and control"; hers is "an India against hegemony", standing for "inclusiveness, secularism, and social justice".

There is a striking concession amid the polemic - she says she understood Modi's "discomfort with the ruling elite of our times".

Sonia says she felt uneasy in Delhi's privileged drawing rooms, where political conversation seemed "very far removed from the reality of India".

Modi's origins, she writes, "may not be as humble as his PR team" suggests, but he "had certainly worked his way to power within the RSS from an underprivileged world". It is a rare acknowledgement of the social distance between the Congress establishment and the electorate Modi came to represent.

The memoir also offers some glimpses of Sonia's encounters with world leaders.

She remembers Vladimir Putin as an "engaging personality" who took her on a boat ride in St Petersburg, pointing out monuments along the way. She says she was impressed by his grasp of geopolitics and his "determination to restore Russia to its former powerful status" - "long before the Ukraine war, a different era".

A more amusing encounter involved France's Nicolas Sarkozy, who arrived in India in 2008 without his then partner Carla Bruni because they were unmarried.

At a state banquet, the Indian vice-president's wife cheerfully grilled him about when he planned to marry her, whether he missed her and whether a date had been fixed. Sarkozy obligingly answered her questions while messaging Bruni on his phone.

Belonging is not a neutral history. The Bofors gun scandal, which badly damaged Rajiv Gandhi's government and dogged the family for decades, gets a relatively brief treatment.

items.title: Real Madrid's Vinícius Jr sends surprise message to boy who lost his legs in Sudan's war
items.summary: Double amputee Zaher told the BBC last year about his favourite footballer and a dream of being able to walk again.
items.content:
In a dark room in Cairo, a 13-year-old boy looks up at a television screen, barely blinking.

The screen flickers and Real Madrid's superstar winger Vinícius Júnior appears addressing the young boy directly, in Arabic: "Zaher, mahaba" - Hello Zaher.

Zaher barely moves, his eyes wide, locked on his favourite footballer.

We first met Zaher a year ago in the ruins of Sudan's capital, Khartoum. He was a small quiet child, scarred by war - one of millions of children whose lives have been upended since the country's army and the paramilitary Rapid Support Forces (RSF) started fighting in 2023.

More than 17 million children are now in need of humanitarian assistance in Sudan, according to the UN children's charity, Unicef. It says it has been able to verify that at least 4,300 have been killed or maimed, although it believes the true figure is far higher.

Zaher had lost both his legs in a drone strike. With little access to specialist treatment, he dreamed of the day he might walk and play football again.

More than a year later, as we walk into an apartment in the Egyptian capital, Zaher greets us with an enormous hug. His mother, Habibah, embraces us too.

The boy we remember as shy and withdrawn is almost unrecognisable. He is confident, cheeky and full of smiles. And he is standing tall on two new prosthetic legs.

For almost a year, Cairo has been his home. Here, he has undergone surgery and months of rehabilitation, and is now able to walk and kick a ball again.

When we met in 2025, he had told us his favourite footballer was Vinícius Júnior. We were able to pass this on to the Real Madrid star, who said he wanted to send a personal video message of support. Reunited in Cairo, we gather round to watch it together.

"I was made aware of your story. I know how difficult the last few months must have been for you," the Brazilian footballer begins.

Vinícius has become a leading voice challenging racism in football and supporting black people, and a smile spreads across Zaher's face as the player tells him: "You are a hard-working black man. I really hope you will make good use of your new prosthetic legs, that you return to playing football and that you find happiness. You deserve it."

Then comes an invitation: "I would like to invite you to attend a Madrid match. We can spend the day together."

Overwhelmed, Zaher gets up and leaves the room. A few moments later, he returns wearing his new Vinícius Jr football shirt. He hopes that one day he will be able to get a visa and accept the offer.

"Tell Vinícius, I love him," he says. "His message has really uplifted me." His mother Habibah says she feels "like the whole world is cheering Zaher on, wanting him to succeed".

Zaher lost his legs in 2024, when he and his mother had been trapped in Khartoum. Much of the city had become a battleground as it was torn apart by fighting between Sudan's army and the RSF.

Food and basic supplies were running short and the family did not have enough money to flee. To survive, they sold lentils on the streets.

Then one morning, as Zaher and his mother worked side by side, a drone struck.

"I looked at him and he was bleeding. There was blood everywhere," Habibah explained last year.

She was devastated. "He would wake up and ask: 'Why did you let them cut off my legs?' I couldn't answer."

Back then, Zaher was wheeling himself through the rubble of his neighbourhood in a wheelchair, past burnt-out cars, abandoned tanks and shattered homes.

Before the war, Zaher had loved football. After the drone strike, he could only play on his knees, a painful process that put him at risk of serious infection.

"I wish I could have prosthetic legs so I can play football with my friends like I used to," he said at the time .

There seemed little prospect of that happening, but his story resonated far beyond Sudan, prompting an outpouring of support from people around the world.

Among them was Dena Latif, a UK-based lawyer of Sudanese origin. After seeing the BBC report, she helped spearhead an online campaign raising £45,000 ($60,000) for his medical care.

Unable to get the treatment he needed in Sudan, Zaher had to leave the country, which was far from straightforward. He and his mother had no passports and their birth certificates had been destroyed during the war.

After months of planning, he and his mother were able to fly to Cairo where an apartment had been prepared for them, with food in the fridge and medical appointments arranged.

For the first time in years, their immediate concern was no longer simply how to survive.

'I can't afford to save both twins': Sudan's war left one mother with an impossible choice

Zaher underwent further surgery, followed by months of physiotherapy and training to learn to use his prosthetic legs. He also received psychological support to help him process the trauma he had been through.

"He was shy, a little bit depressed, sad," says Dr Bintelmuna Eltayeb , one of the doctors involved in his care. "To get a smile out of him was almost impossible, but now you can see he's laughing. He has great confidence in himself."

His transformation has been as much psychological as physical, say those close to him, and Dena says Zaher now approaches life with a determination that has surprised them.

As we spend time with Zaher, he laughs and jokes, making up for some of the childhood that war has taken from him.

He is eager to try new things, from horse riding to cycling, and wants to become an airline pilot. He hasn't had a game of football yet but is looking forward to playing with his friends back home.

For Habibah, watching her son regain his confidence has brought enormous relief. But she worries about his future, his education and how he will be received in Sudan, a country still locked in civil war.

The state of emergency has been lifted in their home city, Khartoum, with the Sudanese army back in control there. But throughout the capital, buildings have been left destroyed - burned, blackened and looted.

Concerns over security remain and 41% of Sudan's population are experiencing high levels of food insecurity, according to a recent statement released by the US and 30 other Western states. The group also warned of "potential famine" .

"I hope that Zaher's story doesn't end with him," says Dena. She hopes his recovery will attract more attention and funds for the thousands of other Sudanese children who have suffered life-altering injuries.

Zaher and his mother are now back in Khartoum. They hope that as the city is more stable at the moment, he will be able to get his prosthetic legs checked and adjusted there as he grows.

Despite the safety they found in Cairo, they missed their home, family and friends. And while Zaher has been given a chance to reclaim his childhood, millions of other Sudanese children are still waiting for theirs.

Additional reporting by Scarlett Barter and Abdelrahman Abutaleb

items.title: 'It can kill us': Kenyans fear impact of El Niño with floods predicted
items.summary: Forecasters warn that this year's El Niño could be one of the strongest on record, with heavy rain and flooding in Kenya.
items.content:
"It flooded up to here in March," Agnes Shikoli says, pointing to a spot halfway up the six-foot [1.8m] corrugated iron wall of her home in Kibera, one of the largest informal settlements in Kenya.

Her tiny house lies just a couple of metres from the Ngong river, which runs through this densely populated area in the capital, Nairobi.

The scars of floods in the long rainy season earlier this year can still be seen - including a broken TV in the corner which was immersed in water.

Tucked out of sight is a photo of her sister Beatrice Khalayi, 58, who died when intense rains caused widespread destruction in Kibera. She was among more than 60 people across the country who lost their lives.

"Someone called me to tell me that she had died of electrocution after her house flooded," Shikoli recalls. "When I see a picture of her, I feel uneasy, that's why I keep it far from me, so I don't see it."

With Kenya's short rainy season now starting, Shikoli tells the BBC she is afraid – especially following warnings that the El Niño weather phenomenon could bring a new round of flooding.

"I feel like it can kill us. These houses aren't made of stone," says the 62-year-old. "They can fall on us, or the water can drown us."

Kibera - and Kenya more widely - are on the frontline of preparations for the potential impact of El Niño.

Forecasters have warned that this year could see one of the strongest on record, bringing extreme weather to many parts of the world.

In southern Kenya, that means the threat of rains even more intense than usual.

Outside Shikoli's house, groups of men and women wearing high-visibility vests are shovelling and raking garbage out of the riverbed and disposing it far from the water.

This programme called Climate Worx, under the office of President William Ruto, is meant to rehabilitate Nairobi's rivers. Such exercises have intensified since August when warnings increased about the possible scale of this year's El Niño .

Similar work to unclog drainage systems is ongoing across Nairobi, a sprawling city built on hilly ground crossed by three major rivers.

Blocked drains and inadequate sewage systems were widely blamed for the high number of deaths after the floods earlier in the year, as the excess rainfall had nowhere to escape.

The Nairobi County disaster management chief, Bramwell Simiyu tells the BBC that drainage systems have been "untouched for many years" and that removing the rubbish from them will save lives.

Floods disproportionately affect informal settlements in Nairobi, especially those near rivers, like Kibera and Mathare.

In most of these settlements, houses sit just a few metres from rivers. Some people, including Shikoli, live on the slopes of the river itself due to the constant expansion of the settlements. When flash floods occur, these houses are swept away, endangering the lives of their occupants.

Nairobi's drainage system hasn't been upgraded to deal with the rapid growth in the population and infrastructure over the decades

"The existing drainage system was developed 30 years ago to cater for a population of about 2.5 million residents but we're dealing with about 7 million in the daytime and 5.5 million night-time," Simiyu says.

He adds that investment of up to $192m (£143m) is needed to upgrade the sewerage and drainage system entirely.

But there is little sign that either the cash-strapped national or city council will able to raise this kind of money.

The Nairobi River Basin Regeneration programme, a government programme aimed at restoring the city's rivers, found that settlements near rivers, and where there is weak enforcement of regulations, have increased flooding risks. It recommended a "buffer" to protect rivers and "humane relocation" of communities where necessary.

However, rising poverty has driven many people to live close to rivers.

"Our worst case scenario looking at low-income settlements is that up to about 100,000 people are at risk," Simiyu says. "Moderate projections is about 5,000 households or about 20,000 people may be at risk."

Anyone forced to leave their homes will be relocated to 167 designated holding grounds where a stockpile of relief food and supplies will be distributed, Simiyu says.

Nobody knows exactly when the rains will come – or how much rain there will be.

But Kenya's meteorological department warns that November is usually the peak rainfall month of the short rainy season, which normally lasts from October to December.

A regional forecast from the Intergovernmental Authority on Development (Igad) warned in September that there was "an 81% probability of a very strong El Niño during October–December 2026".

So far, the heavy rains predicted have not occurred but experts remain concerned.

In East Africa, this El Niño is being widely compared to a similar weather event in 1997-1998 which caused widespread flooding and destruction in Somalia and Kenya.

Weather forecaster Jemima Gacheru tells the BBC that's because temperature conditions in the Indian Ocean in the 1997 El Niño and those recorded now are similar. This interaction, she says, has been seen to result in very strong rainfall.

"For this season we have a very strong El Niño already in play in the Pacific and then we have a positive Indian Ocean dipole," Gacheru said. This is often called the "Indian Niño" because of its similarity to its Pacific equivalent and refers to the difference in sea-surface temperatures in opposite parts of the Indian Ocean .

"We expect to have some enhanced rainfall over several parts of the country."

The UN's migration body the International Organization for Migration (IOM) has warned that almost 900,000 people could be forced to leave their homes in Kenya this year, mostly because of the predicted floods.

Kenya is not the only African country worried about the potential impact of El Niño.

In neighbouring Somalia, the country's disaster management agency has warned that 1.2 million people are at risk of displacement caused by extreme weather – including the risk of both floods and drought.

The 1998 floods killed 2,000 people in Somalia and forced a further 250,000 to flee their homes, according to the Food and Agriculture Organisation. Up to 80% of crops were destroyed in some parts of the country.

The United Nation's famine warning system IPC has warned of the increased risk of food insecurity in Somalia due to supply chain issues exacerbated by the impact of El Niño.

Elsewhere on the continent forecasters fear El Niño could bring extreme heat and prolonged periods without rain.

It could cause a crisis for farmers across parts of West Africa, including the semi-arid Sahel region south of the Sahara, as well as in southern parts of the continent, where the risk of crop failure is high.

There are fears El Niño's impact will worsen existing issues.

Communities like Kibera are already grappling with poor housing and rampant poverty, while parts of Somalia are already in the middle of a devastating drought.

National governments in many countries are doing what they can to prepare but the extent of El Niño's impact is impossible to predict.

Back in Kibera, Shikoli and her family are preparing for the worst.

Council officials have told them they should leave their home on the riverbank until the rainy season has passed but Shikoli makes just $2 (£1.5) a day selling groundnuts and fruit from a small stall next to the river.

items.title: La Camera Usa boccia la procedura di impeachment per Hegseth
items.summary: Trump lo difende: 'E' da 10 e lode'
items.content:
La Camera dei Rappresentanti Usa, a guida repubblicana, ha approvato la mozione che blocca la procedura di impeachment per il segretario alla Difesa Pete Hegseth.

"Il tentativo dei democratici di mettere sotto accusa il Segretario alla Guerra Pete Hegseth è miseramente FALLITO ! Tutti i repubblicani, a eccezione di Thomas Massie, un vero PERDENTE, hanno votato a favore di Pete". Lo scrive Donald Trump su Truth , festeggiando il voto della Camera Usa che ha bocciato la procedura di impeachment.

Il punto poco prima del voto (di Serena Di Ronza) "Un sabotaggio", una "farsa politica". Il capo del Pentagono si presenta combattivo in conferenza stampa per difendersi pubblicamente dalla procedura di impeachment che la Camera si appresta a valutare su richiesta di Thomas Massie, il deputato repubblicano nemico di Donald Trump . In attesa del voto procedurale per stabilire se accantonare la risoluzione o rinviarla all'esame di una commissione, Hegseth ha convocato la sua prima conferenza stampa da maggio e si è presentato combattivo, forte del sostegno di Trump . "E' da 10 e lode", ha detto il presidente Usa ribadendo il suo appoggio per ora incondizionato al capo del Pentagono, colui che all'interno dell'amministrazione gli somiglia di più nei modi.

Hegseth può contare anche sul sostegno del nuovo capo di gabinetto Stephen Miller, anche se molti consiglieri nella Casa Bianca non sanno quanto questo appoggio potrà durare. "Il presidente a un certo punto potrebbe essere costretto a rimuoverlo quando la situazione non sarà più sostenibile", hanno osservato alcune fonti con Cnn. A essere sicuro che Hegseth lascerà o il commander-in-chief lo silurerà è il senatore repubblicano Ted Cruz, convinto che la Camera "molto probabilmente, se non di sicuro" approverà il suo impeachment. I deputati si avviano al voto procedurale, che stabilità se andare avanti con la procedura o meno. Una volta superato questo scoglio la Camera potrebbe esprimersi direttamente sulla risoluzione di impeachment. Se dovesse essere approvata, la palla passerebbe al Senato che dovrebbe procedere con il processo e con un voto che necessità due terzi dei voti della camera Alta per la destituzione di Hegseth. Le probabilità che questo accada sono remote.

Nella storia americana nessuno ministro della Difesa è mai stato messo in stato d'accusa. Gli sforzi per l'impeachment sono una "farsa. Sono motivati dalla politica e si fanno beffa della costituzione", ha detto senza mezzi termine Hegseth durante la sua conferenza stampa al Pentagono. Trenta minuti in cui è apparso ansioso, sulla difensiva e quasi esasperato dagli attacchi. Chi dice che le forze armate americane hanno preso di mira dei civili dice "calunnie. Gli unici che prendono di mira i civili sono i terroristi", ha spiegato cercando di smontare le accuse nei suoi confronti. Presentandosi come difensore delle forze armate, Hegseth ha osservato che "se vogliono prendersela con i nostri soldati guerrieri, allora dovranno prima superare me".

Poi ha ringraziato Trump per il sostegno. "Gli sono grato. Ha fatto la cosa giusta" in Iran "non per calcoli politici ma per la sicurezza degli americani. Questa è leadership", ha messo in evidenza dicendosi d'accordo con il presidente quando dice che "rifarebbe la guerra in Iran" . Dal podio ha elencato i suoi successi in Venezuela in "soli 48 minuti" e in Medio Oriente, in quelle che ha definito tutte "operazioni perfettamente legali", criticate da un deputato "insoddisfatto" che vuole uno "spettacolo politico per il suo ego e perché ha del risentimento". Massie è nemico giurato di Trump che, prendendo di mira Hegseth, punta a far male al presidente privandolo di un fedelissimo. Difendendosi a spada tratta e criticando il deputato repubblicano autore della risoluzione di impeachment, Hegseth ha anche esortato il Congresso ad approvare i fondi necessari affinché il Pentagono possa continuare a operare regolarmente. Il ministro della Difesa è consapevole che il budget del suo dipartimento potrebbe diventare un'arma per fermare la guerra in Iran : privando il Pentagono dei fondi necessari, infatti, il conflitto dovrebbe fermarsi.

La guerra in Iran è uno dei motivi per cui i repubblicani hanno perso alle elezioni di metà mandato , e una delle ragioni di spaccatura all'interno dell'amministrazione. Il vicepresidente JD Vance, contrario fin dall'inizio al conflitto , ha difeso Hegseth senza far riferimento all'Iran. Il segretario di Stato, Marco Rubio, si è limitato a dire che ha seguito gli ordini di Trump. Prese di posizioni caute da parte dei due papabili candidati al 2028 che, pur dovendo mostrare fedeltà a Trump e all'amministrazione, evitano di parlare di quella guerra in Iran che sta mettendo a rischio le loro ambizioni politiche.

items.title: The DRAM interface and the PHY (why a DDR3+ interface must be tuned at boot)
items.summary: Article URL: https://github.com/enjoy-digital/litedram/blob/master/doc/manual/03_dram_interface.md Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50447900 Points: 4 # Comments: 0
items.content:
This chapter explains what happens on the wires between the FPGA and the DRAM, and why a DRAM interface must be tuned at boot. It covers the signals, the strobes, the board topology, the leveling procedures, the termination and the reference voltages, then the clocks of the FPGA and the DFI interface between the controller and the PHY.

Each section ends with the part of LiteDRAM that implements the mechanism. The previous chapter, DRAM in a nutshell , explained the commands and the timings; Initialization and calibration gives the exact steps the BIOS runs.

A DRAM interface has two halves. The command and address half goes one way, from the controller to the DRAM, and is shared by every chip of a rank. The data half is bidirectional and split into byte lanes , each with its own strobe. The figure below shows the signals.

A byte lane is 8 DQ, their DQS pair and their DM. Each lane is routed on its own, so each one can arrive at a slightly different time, and each one is tuned on its own.

In LiteDRAM, the pads of the DRAM are a record from the platform file, with fields named after these signals ( dq , dqs_p , a , ba , cs_n ). The PHY counts the lanes from it. Two helpers of litedram/common.py reshape the pads: PHYPadsReducer keeps some lanes only, and PHYPadsCombiner merges chips with separate command buses into one controller.

SDR memory transfers one word per clock, sampled on the rising edge of the clock that the controller sends. DDR memories transfer two words per clock, one on each edge, and at these rates the clock from the controller cannot be trusted to sample the data: the delays of the board and of the chips are too large.

The data therefore travel with their own clock, the strobe DQS: the side that sends the data also sends DQS, and the receiver samples DQ with it. This is a source-synchronous interface. Both travel the same path, so their delays cancel. The figure below shows how DQS is aligned with DQ.

On writes the controller sends DQS centre aligned , its edges in the middle of each bit. On reads the DRAM sends DQS edge aligned , on the bit transitions, and the receiver delays it by a quarter of a clock. Before the burst, DQS is driven for a preamble , and after it for a postamble , without carrying data.

In LiteDRAM, the DDR PHYs shift the write DQS by a quarter of a clock from DQ, with the means of its FPGA:

DDR3 and DDR4 route the clock, command and address pins as one bus that passes by every chip in turn and ends on a termination: the fly-by topology. It keeps these heavily loaded signals clean at high rates, but each chip receives the clock a little later than the previous one. The figure below shows it.

The data lanes are point to point, so their delays do not follow the clock. A chip needs DQS to arrive close to its own CK edge (tDQSS). With fly-by routing the skew between the first and the last chip can exceed a clock period, so each lane needs its own DQS delay.

Write leveling measures that delay. The controller sets the DRAM into write leveling mode with a mode register bit (MR1 bit A7 on DDR3 and DDR4), then sends DQS pulses. The DRAM samples its CK with each DQS rising edge and returns the sampled value on DQ. The controller delays DQS step by step until DQ goes from 0 to 1: DQS is then aligned with CK at that chip.

In LiteDRAM, the PHYs expose write leveling through registers: wlevel_en enables the mode, wlevel_strobe sends one DQS pulse, and per-lane output delays move DQS and DQ. The BIOS runs the scan ( sdram_write_leveling in liblitedram ).

Write leveling needs output delays: the Kintex-7 and Virtex-7 PHYs in HP banks and the UltraScale PHYs have them. The Artix-7 has none: with one static DQS phase, only some lanes of a fly-by memory meet tDQSS. Its optional CK phase shift mode ( with_ck_phase_shift , DDR3 at 1:4) moves CK against all the lanes instead ( CK phase shift ).

Write leveling aligns DQS with CK within one clock period, but a lane can be one whole clock early or late: the DRAM then writes the burst shifted by a few words. Write latency calibration writes a known pattern, reads it back, and moves each lane by whole clocks until the pattern is right.

DQ-DQS training then centres DQ against DQS on writes. It sweeps the output delay of the DQ pins of each lane, writes and reads back a pattern at each step, and keeps the middle of the passing range. It relies on a working read side, which read leveling then refines.

In LiteDRAM, the write latency is moved by write bitslips ( wdly_dq_bitslip ) and DQ by output delays ( wdly_dq ). Each PHY declares which calibrations it supports in its settings ( write_leveling , write_latency_calibration , write_dq_dqs_training , read_leveling ); the BIOS runs only those.

On reads, the controller does not know when the data arrive. The DRAM answers CL clocks after RD, but the board and the I/Os add a delay that differs per lane. Two settings must be found for each lane: a coarse one, which fast clock cycle holds the first word, and a fine one, where in the bit to sample.

The coarse setting is a bitslip : the deserializer output is shifted by whole bits until the words line up. The fine setting is an input delay, from a few picoseconds to about a hundred per step depending on the FPGA (78 ps on 7-Series with a 200 MHz reference). Read leveling writes a pattern, then for each bitslip sweeps the delay and reads the pattern back. The figure below shows such a scan.

The window is the data eye seen through the delay line. A wide window means a robust interface; a narrow one points to a signal integrity or clocking problem. DDR3 and DDR4 can also return a fixed pattern from their MPR (multi-purpose register), so the read side can be tuned before anything has been written.

The PHYs that capture with DQS have one more problem: DQS is not driven between bursts, so the receiver must listen to it only during a read. The FPGA's DQS block opens this gate and reports a burst detect, which read leveling uses to confirm that the read window is right.

In LiteDRAM, each PHY declares its number of delay taps and bitslips in its settings ( delays , bitslips ), and exposes them through registers ( rdly_dq_inc , rdly_dq_bitslip , and burstdet_seen on the Lattice and Gowin PHYs). The BIOS runs the scan and prints one line per lane and bitslip. On DDR4 it reads the MPR patterns, except on registered DIMMs and clamshell layouts.

At DRAM rates, a signal reflects at the end of a line that is not terminated. The DRAM therefore terminates its own data pins with an on-die termination (ODT): a resistor switched on when the ODT pin is high. The FPGA terminates its inputs in the same way when it receives read data.

DDR3 and DDR4 have two termination values: RTT_NOM, used when the chip is idle or another rank is written, and RTT_WR, used while the chip itself is written ( dynamic ODT ). The driver strength of the DRAM, RON, sets how hard it drives the read data. All three are set in the mode registers.

In LiteDRAM, the defaults of the table are set by litedram/init.py ; a PHY can override them ( rtt_nom , rtt_wr , ron in its settings). With the DRAM DLL off, a DDR3 mode for low clock rates that the GW5A PHY offers ( dll_off ), both terminations are disabled.

The ODT pin is driven statically by default. With with_dynamic_odt (DDR3, single rank), the controller raises ODT only around writes, so the DRAM terminations are off during reads ( Dynamic ODT ). The FPGA side termination is part of the I/O standards of the platform file, not of LiteDRAM.

The resistance of the drivers and terminations of a chip varies with the process, the voltage and the temperature. DDR3 and later chips calibrate them against a precision resistor on their ZQ pin, 240 ohm to ground. ZQCL, the long calibration, runs once at initialization; ZQCS, the short one, corrects the drift from time to time during operation.

In LiteDRAM, the initialization sequence ends with ZQCL ( Mode registers and power-up ), and the refresher sends ZQCS once per second by default ( Refresh ). LPDDR4 has no ZQCS: it calibrates with two multi-purpose commands (MPC), start and latch, which LiteDRAM sends at initialization only.

The data receivers compare each input to a reference voltage, VREF, set halfway between the high and the low levels. On DDR3 the board provides VREF on dedicated pins. DDR4 terminates its data pins to the supply (pseudo open drain), so the data swing sits near the top of the supply and the right reference is not halfway. The DRAM generates its data VREF internally, programmed in MR6.

On the FPGA side, the receivers of the read data also need a VREF. Some FPGA I/O banks can set it internally, in steps, instead of using a VREF pin.

In LiteDRAM, the DDR4 initialization writes MR6 with tCCD_L only and leaves its VREF field at zero, the first value of range 1 (60% of VDDQ): the DRAM data VREF is not trained.

The UltraScale+ PHY can set the FPGA read VREF of its HP I/O banks ( with_hpio_vref , register rd_vref , codes 0 to 72). The BIOS does not scan it: the register keeps its build-time value ( hpio_vref_tune ) unless software writes it. LiteX issue 2769 tracks the missing BIOS sweep.

items.title: Tensione sulle armi all'Ucraina, la Lega avvisa gli alleati
items.summary: Risolto il giallo della mancata firma di Giorgetti. Meloni: 'Lo farà appena rientra a Roma'
items.content:
La mancata firma di Giancarlo Giorgetti sul pacchetto di forniture militari all'Ucraina è stata legata a "un impedimento fisico temporaneo". Il ministro siglerà il decreto interministeriale, "quando tornerà a Roma". Giorgia Meloni prova così ad assicurare che "non c'è alcuna questione". Minimizza le barricate della Lega (rilanciate da Claudio Borghi con un avvertimento sull'eventuale nuovo decreto per il 2027) , che rientrano nella categoria "sensibilità diverse", di fronte alle quali la maggioranza ha "sempre trovato una sintesi". E comunque "la posizione dell'Italia non cambierà".

Ma tutto è nato proprio dalla puntualizzazione della Lega, sull'onda dell'irritazione per aver ascoltato Antonio Tajani affermare che lui e Giorgetti avevano già controfirmato il decreto interministeriale . Una grana, quantomeno a livello di comunicazione, proprio alla vigilia dei colloqui ad Abu Dhabi, a cui l'Italia ha partecipato nel formato europeo E4 (per il M5s "il nuovo pacchetto di armi a Kiev è stato il biglietto d'ingresso"). E a ridosso di un'altra partita interna aperta, la scelta del presidente dell'Autorità nazionale anticorruzione ("Se non è di sinistra non lo possiamo mettere all'Anac?", la risposta della premier a un giornalista che chiedeva se un uomo della Lega possa ricoprire il ruolo). La premier a stretto giro aveva sentito al telefono il ministro dell'Economia, che le avrebbe spiegato di non aver potuto leggere e firmare il documento secretato perché da diversi giorni fuori da Roma. Reduce da un intervento alla schiena e poi dall'Ecofin a Bruxelles , dovrebbe tornare nella Capitale fra mercoledì e giovedì e a quel punto lo firmerà.

"Non ci saranno sorprese", assicura il ministro della Difesa Guido Crosetto. Il problema politico, però, resta. Perché mentre Meloni parla con i giornalisti a Bologna, prima di visitare l'Esposizione internazionale di macchine per l'agricoltura e il giardinaggio, a Roma il ministro Crosetto illustra al Copasir i contenuti del tredicesimo pacchetto di aiuti militari a Kiev. "Un decreto che non c'è (perché un atto che richiede il concerto con diversi ministri finché non viene firmato dai medesimi non esiste)" , nota il componente leghista Borghi, esponendo la linea di Matteo Salvini, un avvertimento in vista della scadenza dell'annuale legge cornice per inviare forniture all'Ucraina.

"Qualora si volesse fare un decreto per il 2027, cosa che io sconsiglio, a quel punto - la puntualizzazione del fedelissimo del segretario - c'è una contrarietà politica che è stata raccontata e data come mandato al congresso della Lega ". Anche l'anno scorso ci fu un braccio di ferro fra la Lega (Roberto Vannacci allora era vicesegretario) e gli alleati, chiuso con un escamotage lessicale che dava "priorità" agli aiuti "logistici, sanitari, a d uso civile e di protezione dagli attacchi aerei, missilistici, con droni e cibernetici".

Da FdI, Giovanni Donzelli auspica che "non ci sia bisogno" di un altro decreto e "che si arrivi alla pace, ma - sottolinea - non ci siamo mai sottratti dal fare la nostra parte". Nel governo domina la speranza che entro fine anno si chiuda il conflitto. A partire da Meloni, da tempo consapevole che l'appoggio a Kiev ha "un prezzo politico", e che una parte del suo elettorato non lo condivide. "Per noi è un vanto aver sempre avuto una posizione chiara - rivendica la premier pungendo le opposizioni -. Non so come andrebbe con altri al governo...".

"Il sostegno dell'Italia è garantito", puntualizza anche Antonio Tajani. E Crosetto chiede alla politica di non affrontare "la questione Ucraina con le maglie delle squadre ". Intanto la presentazione al Copasir del pacchetto e la firma di Giorgetti sono gli ultimi due passaggi formali prima dell'invio delle forniture. La lista è come sempre secretata, ma a una domanda sull'eventuale mancanza di missili Aster, i l ministro della Difesa ha osservato: "ne abbiamo da tenere per noi".

items.title: Nvidia hires major US law firm to investigate alleged Chinese spy affair
items.summary: The appointment was made after it emerged Jensen Huang had an affair with a woman believed to be a spy for China.
items.content:
Nvidia has hired one of the largest law firms in the US to investigate the affair between its own chief executive and an alleged Chinese spy.

Jensen Huang, who co-founded the tech company, has admitted to having a romantic relationship outside of his marriage. The woman, Alice Huang, is alleged to be a spy for Beijing.

Nvidia said on Tuesday that it had hired New York law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz, and that its attorney Joon Kim would lead "a thorough and independent investigation". The FBI is also conducting its own probe .

The company's share price has fallen almost to a yearly low, with $500bn (£375bn) wiped of its stock market value since Friday.

Nvidia is widely considered one of the most important companies behind the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, given it is the sole manufacturer of a computer chip used in AI tools.

It is the world's second most valuable company after Apple and its chips have become a matter of national security for US officials who are keen to win the AI race.

Alice Huang, who is also known as Huang Le, and is not related to Jensen Huang, was an executive at Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has been a customer of Nvidia.

Megaspeed had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia has said was investigated and debunked.

Nvidia has also maintained that the US government did not inform it that Megaspeed posed an intelligence concern.

What we know so far about Jensen Huang's affair with suspected Chinese spy

Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond

According to the New York Times, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington earlier this year warning that Jensen Huang was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Beijing has rejected claims that the Nvidia chief has been targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "intended to smear and malign China".

US President Donald Trump said on Monday that he had spoken to Jensen Huang, who had said he had "no idea she was a spy." Trump said he believed him.

However, the relationship has drawn more political attention. Congressional leaders of the House Committee on Foreign Affairs have asked Huang to appear next week for a closed door briefing.

The Nvidia boss has yet to say whether he will attend, a person familiar with the committee's demand told the BBC. The committee has the authority to subpoena Huang, effectively forcing him to appear before it, if deemed necessary.

When announcing on Sunday that it would investigate the affair, Nvidia's board said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

It added that a committee of independent directors would oversee the probe.

Wachtell is one of the largest law firms in the US and has several notable clients in the tech industry. Among them are OpenAI and Salesforce.

Joon Kim is a former US Attorney for New York's Southern District and spent several years working as a government attorney focusing on fraud and other criminal acts.

The Nvidia investigation will likely be treated as urgent, according to sources familiar with the matter, as Jensen Huang's public image is tightly intertwined with the company.

He has become a key public figure in the development on AI, arguing the technology is a "new industrial revolution" and is on par with the advent of electricity.

It is unclear, however, if Wachtell will be able to interview Alice Huang.

A spokesperson for Nvidia declined to comment on Tuesday when asked if Jensen Huang had retained any of his own legal representation amid the company investigation and the separate one launched by the FBI.

items.title: Il Change Bloc trova i numeri con gli arabi alla Knesset, ma è rebus governo
items.summary: Intesa su Kahana alla presidenza. L'ira di Netanyahu, Eisenkot annulla incontro col Likud
items.content:
La sessione inaugurale della 26ª Knesset si è aperta all'insegna del paradosso che definisce l'attuale stallo istituzionale : il Change Bloc incassa la prima vittoria, portando 67 firme per anticipare, al 17 novembre, l'elezione del nuovo presidente .

Per farlo, inaugura la prima collaborazione con i partiti arabi, tutti uniti nel sostenere il candidato del partito Yashar di Gadi Eisenkot, Matan Kahana , che, avendo servito come vice speaker in passato, si reputa abbia le spalle sufficientemente solide per affrontare la fase da 'anatra zoppa' che si prospetta. Una collaborazione su cui però continua a pendere come una spada di Damocle il veto assoluto di Avigdor Liberman a un governo con i partiti arabi, anche solo come supporto esterno. Le due strade quindi, quella parlamentare e quella governativa, viaggiano ancora su binari diversi, e non è chiaro se e come convergeranno.

Al primo binario si aggiunge anche il blitz parlamentare su cui intende procedere il Change Bloc, che ha depositato una serie di leggi, a partire da quella per l'istituzione di una commissione d'inchiesta sui fatti che hanno portato al massacro del 7 ottobre 2023, e quella ad hoc contro Netanyahu , volta a introdurre un limite ai mandati per il premier. Anche qui verrà misurata la fiducia tra le varie anime che formano il gruppo determinato a chiudere l'era Netanyahu, che va in parallelo con il do ut des per la formazione dell'esecutivo. I numeri che oggi blindano la presidenza della Knesset sono infatti il frutto di un accordo puramente tecnico, un 'matrimonio di convenienza' per sbloccare l'impasse istituzionale iniziale. Quando l'orizzonte si sposta sulla stesura di un programma di governo, le crepe all'interno del Change Bloc emergono in tutta la loro imponenza.

Mansour Abbas, il leader del partito islamico Ra'am con 8 seggi sembra propenso a riconoscere Hamas come organizzazione terroristica , acconsentendo ai prerequisiti posti da Eisenkot. Per farlo, vuole garanzie su ruoli significativi nell'esecutivo. Sull'altra sponda, vanno avanti i negoziati condotti da Liberman per incassare i 7 seggi del partito ultraortodosso Ebraismo Unito, che chiede una legge sull'arruolamento ancora più lassista di quella formulata dagli ex alleati del blocco della destra, e quindi difficile da digerire per il Change Bloc che aveva fatto della questione un cardine elettorale.

Netanyahu non rinuncia agli ultraortodossi, e ha tenuto un lungo incontro notturno con il leader del partito Yaakov Asher. Un corteggiamento bipartisan che altro non fa che aumentarne la potenza negoziale. Il premier uscente ha sfruttato la sede istituzionale della Knesset per quello che sembrava quasi un comizio elettorale, sentendosi forte dell'impasse in cui si muovono gli avversari. Ha ribadito la necessità dell'unità nazionale e al contempo continuato con la veemente delegittimazione dei deputati arabi e dei leader del Change Bloc, che gli sedevano davanti durante l'invettiva. Tanto che Eisenkot, parlando di "discorso delirante", ha annullato un incontro del suo team negoziale con il Likud, previsto per domani. Un punto di osservazione interessante arriva da una "fonte diplomatica di un Paese arabo con cui Israele intrattiene rapporti diplomatici", riportata da Channel 11: meglio un governo di Eisenkot con gli ultraortodossi che un esecutivo che abbia ancora i ministri oltranzisti Itamar Ben Gvir e Bezalel Smotrich. "Gli haredim (i religiosi) sono un partner comodo, meglio di quelle figure intransigenti con le loro ambizioni territoriali regionali", è stato riferito.

items.title: L'ex Br Bertulazzi scappa dai domiciliari a Buenos Aires, è caccia all'uomo
items.summary: Era un passo dall'estradizione, l'Interpol era pronta a riportarlo in Italia
items.content:
L'ex Br Leonardo Bertulazzi, di 74 anni, è scappato dagli arresti domiciliari in cui si trovava a Buenos Aires. Lo ha confermato all'ANSA il suo avvocato, Rodolfo Yanzon . La Direzione Generale dell'Intelligence Criminale ha emesso un allarme urgente per rintracciarlo immediatamente.

Bertulazzi si trovava agli arresti domiciliari in un appartamento nel quartiere San Telmo, nel centro di Buenos Aires. Dopo la revoca del suo status di rifugiato, è riuscito a sottrarsi alle autorità e a fuggire, dando immediatamente il via a una caccia all'uomo a livello nazionale . Prima della fuga, la giustizia argentina aveva respinto anche l'ultimo ricorso contro l'estradizione - che questa volta aveva presentato per motivi di salute - e l'Interpol, secondo quanto riferisce lo stesso Yanzon, era già pronta a prelevare l'ex Br per portarlo in Italia . "La legge argentina stabilisce chiaramente che, per motivi di salute, qualora le condizioni di una persona non lo consentano , quest'ultima non può essere trasferita. Si tratta di uno dei presupposti in base ai quali un'estradizione può essere sospesa", ha tuttavia sottolineato il difensore.

"Leonardo non godeva di buona salute e, durante la detenzione nel corso di questo procedimento, è stato colpito per tre volte da un ictus", ha riferito Yanzon. "L'ultimo accertamento a cui è stato sottoposto risale allo scorso venerdì 6 novembre, presso il centro per l'epilessia dell'ospedale Ramón Mejía . Gli è stato prescritto un ciclo di cure della durata di due mesi e sono stati disposti alcuni esami medici; il primo di questi, un elettroencefalogramma, era stato fissato per il 27 novembre" . "Questa era la situazione quando ne ho informato Bertulazzi; lui indubbiamente ha preso una decisione difficile - quella di fuggire - che io accolgo ad ogni modo con favore dato che il giudice che si occupa del caso, Maria Servini de Cubria, non è stata all'altezza della situazione", ha concluso Yanzon.

Bertulazzi è stato condannato in via definitiva a 27 anni per il sequestro dell'industriale Pietro Costa e per banda armata. E' stato arrestato nel 2024 dopo 44 anni di latitanza in Sudamerica. Negli anni '70 faceva parte della colonna genovese delle Brigate Rosse e ha partecipato al sequestro dell'ingegnere Pietro Costa, la cui famiglia pagò un miliardo di lire di riscatto. Somma che servì ai Br per acquistare l'appartamento di via Montalcini a Roma che l'anno successivo diventerà la prigione di Aldo Mor o. Arrestato una prima volta nel 2002, Bertulazzi era stato liberato da parte di un tribunale dell'Argentina, poiché il Paese non consente l'estradizione nei casi di condanna di un imputato in contumacia. Buenos Aires nel frattempo aveva concesso al terrorista lo status di rifugiato politico, poi revocato nel 2024 sotto il governo di Javier Milei.

items.title: After 7 Months, Glasswing Overwelms Maintainers with Underwhelming Findings
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.vulncheck.com/blog/anthropic-glasswing-november-update Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50447074 Points: 118 # Comments: 37
items.content:
We're seven months into Anthropic's flagship Project Glasswing, and it's time for another update on the results. I've been tracking the project to see whether its claims are overhyped or grounded in reality.

As we all recall, Anthropic launched Project Glasswing on April 7th, claiming, "We have identified thousands of additional high- and critical-severity vulnerabilities that we are working on responsibly disclosing to open source maintainers." What surprised me was how little evidence the project offered, which made me wonder whether this was more of an overhyped marketing campaign.

That said, we shouldn't overlook that AI is an effective tool for finding vulnerabilities. But that story goes well beyond any single frontier model's capabilities.

If you're just catching up, this builds on my earlier posts:

I started tracking Anthropic's discovered vulnerabilities on April 17th, shortly after launch, in an open source repo called code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> Anthropic Credited CVEs . The goal was to see whether Anthropic's claims lived up to the hype. This was before Anthropic launched its own code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> disclosure ledger , which is only updated in infrequent bulk batches.

My repo tracks every vulnerability attributable to Anthropic using CVE records, GHSAs, Linux kernel commits, and Anthropic's own ledger. I also manually audit advisories to catch CVEs that might otherwise get overlooked.

After seven months, I've tracked 442 CVEs attributable to Anthropic. That's an average of just 63 per month. Out of the 93,450 CVEs published this year, that's only about 0.5% of all CVEs.

For comparison, Anthropic's own public ledger lists just 217 fixed vulnerabilities, so I've tracked more than twice as many as Anthropic has disclosed itself.

You may recall that Glasswing launched with the message that we'd entered the Mythos era of vulnerability discovery. But are these vulnerabilities actually useful to attackers? To find out, I've been tracking Anthropic-discovered CVEs against VulnCheck KEV. So far, only 2 of the 442 have been exploited in the wild, just 0.45%. (CVE-2026-61500 and CVE-2026-26980)

When Anthropic first launched its ledger in May, it reported 23,019 findings and a 90.8% true positive rate. As of its most recent update on November 2nd, there are 37,966 findings and just 217 fixes. That looks like a staggering failure to me, but let's take a closer look.

Of the 37,966 findings Anthropic reports, only 7,349 (19.4%) have been made public. Just 217 of those have been marked fixed. The more glaring number is that 4.4% (1,654) of the project's findings have already been marked as duplicates, 7.5x more duplicates than fixes. On top of that, 419 findings have been withdrawn. It seems odd that the ledger now claims a 94.2% true positive rate, up from 90.8% at launch, when more findings have been withdrawn or marked as duplicates than fixed, likely a feedback loop missing to the triage rates listed as “True Positives”.

In two months, Anthropic added nearly 12,000 findings and fixed just 15 more. Duplicates went from two to thousands, which is exactly what I warned about in September: the longer findings sit, the more likely someone else finds and fixes them first. I don't know how anyone can read these numbers as anything but damning.

You may also notice a correction in my visual. There appears to be a bug on Anthropic's ledger that inflates the number of findings marked as disclosed. Check for yourself using the "disclosed" filter.

Having humans triage every finding clearly didn't scale, and Anthropic has said as much. In its code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> OSS Scanner launch post on October 8th, Anthropic said it had found more than 29,000 candidate vulnerabilities but had manually reviewed only about 6,000, and that it remains "bottlenecked on our human capacity to validate these findings." It had also already sent nearly 5,000 unverified reports to maintainers who asked for everything in bulk.

So with the Glasswing open source initiative hitting a wall, launching a self-service code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> OSS Scanner that projects can opt into makes sense. Maintainers can now request a scan and triage the findings themselves. Anthropic is upfront that these reports are "fully model-generated, without human review or triage" and that "it is possible reports will be incorrect or invalid."

In other words, the triage bottleneck didn't go away. It moved to the maintainers. If the true positive rate is really as high as Anthropic claims, that shouldn't be a problem.

Three days ago, code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> Daniel Stenberg , who maintains curl, code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> announced that the project had received a batch of 45 vulnerability reports from Anthropic. Anthropic rated only one as medium severity and the rest as low. Daniel is moving them over to GitHub at a deliberate pace "to soften the impact for the team," with plans to have them all published by the end of the week. This gives us a rare look at what Anthropic's findings look like once a maintainer actually validates them.

Of the 34 reports published so far, 19 have been marked as not a vulnerability, 6 have been confirmed as low severity, and 9 are still awaiting assessment. That puts the false positive rate at 55.9% so far, and only 17.6% of findings have been confirmed, all of them low severity. That's a lot of work dumped on open source maintainers for a small handful of low-impact bugs, and when a maintainer has to pace reports just to protect his team, that says plenty about the burden.

This also isn't new for curl. Back in May, Daniel code]:outline-0 [&>code]:border-dashed [&>code]:outline-primary/25 focus-visible:[&>code]:outline-3 hover:[&>code]:border-primary hover:[&>code]:text-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:border-primary focus-visible:[&>code]:text-primary transition-colors [&>code]:transition-colors"> wrote that five Mythos findings boiled down to a single confirmed vulnerability.

It's a far cry from the 94.2% true positive rate Anthropic currently claims on its ledger. It also undercuts the "high- and critical-severity" framing Glasswing launched with. In September, I found that Claude rated 91.5% of ledger findings as critical or high, while maintainers rated only 51.3% that way. I'm curious whether other open source projects are seeing the same thing.

curl took a bold move by deciding to publish low and medium vulnerabilities findings publicly as issues for full transparency and we encourage other open source maintainers to follow their lead.

AI is a valuable tool for finding vulnerabilities, and I'm not discounting that. But seven months in, the evidence still doesn't match the launch narrative. The CVEs are a sliver of this year's total, almost none are being exploited, fixes have stalled while duplicates and withdrawals pile up, and the triage burden is shifting onto the open source maintainers Glasswing promised to help. The receipts keep coming in. They still don't reconcile.

VulnCheck is helping organizations not just to solve the vulnerability prioritization challenge - we’re working to help equip any product manager, CSIRT/PSIRT or SecOps team and Threat Hunting team to get faster and more accurate with infinite efficiency using VulnCheck solutions.

We knew that we needed better data, faster across the board, in our industry. So that’s what we deliver to the market. We’re going to continue to deliver key insights on vulnerability management, exploitation and major trends we can extrapolate from our dataset to continuously support practitioners.

items.title: Meghan's father Thomas Markle back in federal custody after allegedly removing ankle monitor
items.summary: The 82-year-old was placed under house detention in Florida last week after being charged over possession of child sex abuse material.
items.content:
Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan, Duchess of Sussex, is back in federal custody in Florida after allegedly removing his ankle monitor, according to court documents.

Markle appeared before a federal magistrate judge in the Florida city of Tampa on Tuesday and was denied bond. Prosecutors say he removed the monitor early that morning.

US Judge Lindsay S Griffin found on Tuesday that Markle had violated the conditions of his pretrial release, court documents show.

Markle, who has denied possessing images of child sex abuse, was arrested in Florida last week and placed under house detention. He was also ordered to wear a location monitoring device.

Griffin described Markle's housing situation as "untenable", writing in the order revoking his pretrial release that "based on the lack of suitable housing, no condition or combination of conditions would reasonably assure the safety of any other person or the community and the defendant's appearance in court".

He also ordered a medical evaluation for Markle and said he "must receive all necessary and prescribed medication unless discontinued by a physician".

"Release conditions are court orders, not suggestions," Bill Essayli, the US attorney for Central California, wrote on X on Tuesday.

"We will continue to prosecute this case to the fullest extent of the law," he added.

Markle, 82, was first arrested last week after the FBI, acting on warrants, searched storage units in Los Angeles registered to him which he had rented since 2008, with the last payment being made in October this year, the DoJ said.

Inside the units the FBI says agents seized about 78 items, including film negatives, slides and books that they allege contained child sex abuse material.

Witnesses "positively identified" Markle in two of the images believed to contain child sex abuse material.

In those images, the man pictured "appears to be in the age range of 30s to 40s", which suggests the alleged abuse dates back decades as Markle is currently 82 years old.

Markle appeared in court last week following his arrest. No plea was taken during the appearance, which set several conditions for his pretrial release, including that he be kept in home detention.

He is charged with one count of possessing indecent images of children, according to the DoJ.

FBI director Kash Patel said last week that Markle "allegedly targeted innocent children and sought to steal their innocence through his criminal actions".

He moved to the Philippines last year after he had a series of strokes, and lived in Cebu until May. He was reportedly learning to walk again in Florida after having his leg amputated.

The duchess has been estranged from her father since 2018. The BBC understands she broke contact with him last year, telling him she and the authorities knew he had abused young girls.

In a previously shared statement, Meghan confirmed the existence of the letter and wrote: "I am deeply distressed... my thoughts are with any children who may have been harmed."

She said she hoped it could be understood why she had largely cut off contact from her father and did "not allow him to have contact with our children".

items.title: Il trapper Baby Gang non va in udienza, 'pestato in carcere'
items.summary: L'episodio riferito al suo legale. A processo per un mitra mostrato in un video
items.content:
Non si è presentato oggi in udienza a Lecco, per uno dei suoi processi, il trapper Baby Gang, 25 anni all'anagrafe Zaccaria Mouhib, perché il giovane ha riferito al suo difensore di essere stato "pestato in carcere".

Il suo legale, l'avvocato Niccolò Vecchioni, lo ha fatto presente al giudice, che ha acquisito una relazione medica del carcere di Busto Arsizio (Varese) che, come spiegato dalla difesa, dava atto di "segni di percosse riferiti dal detenuto". Il cantante è a processo in abbreviato, davanti al gup Salvatore Catalano, assieme all'amico e trapper Simba La Rue, ossia Lamine Saida, per il possesso di un fucile mitragliatore esibito nel video di un brano di Baby Gang, al quale aveva preso parte anche Simba. Nella scorsa udienza la pm Chiara Stoppioni ha chiesto la condanna a due anni e quattro mesi per Baby Gang e a un anno e otto mesi per Simba La Rue.

Il 25enne ha partecipato all'udienza in videocollegamento dal carcere. Udienza che è stata dedicata agli interventi della difesa, mentre la sentenza è prevista per gennaio. Il trapper era stato arrestato nuovamente il 17 marzo in un'altra inchiesta della Procura lecchese per accuse di detenzione di armi e altri reati chiusa nei mesi scorsi. Il 13 novembre al Riesame di Milano si discuterà la richiesta della difesa di concessione dei domiciliari in una comunità terapeutica, con braccialetto elettronico, per un "disturbo psichiatrico" e per "abuso di stupefacenti".

items.title: rVPN – stealth VPN with end-to-end encryption
items.summary: Article URL: https://rvpn.org/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50446714 Points: 54 # Comments: 44
items.content:
rVPN is an open-source protocol that carries your traffic safely across the internet, indistinguishable from ordinary HTTPS, so it works even where VPNs are blocked.

We believe privacy should be proven, not promised . Every line is open to read, audit, and run yourself.

A censor watching the wire sees ordinary web traffic on port 443. No tell-tale handshake, no blockable fingerprint. If they probe the server, it answers like a normal website.

A Double Ratchet rekeys every message, so a stolen key never unlocks the past or the future.

Probe the endpoint and it serves a real decoy site. Nothing to confirm, nothing to block.

The core is written in Rust, so entire classes of vulnerability cannot occur.

One TLS connection per flow means hundreds of parallel sessions under load: slow to establish, and a shape worth flagging. Pooled multiplexing carries every flow over a handful of long-lived connections, so the wire stays small and ordinary no matter how busy you are.

Every flow pays a full TCP + TLS + WebSocket + X3DH handshake. A busy client holds hundreds of parallel TLS sessions to one server.

Flows share a small pool of long-lived connections. Credit-based flow control keeps bulk transfers from starving interactive ones, and reconnects resume TLS 1.3 tickets in a single round trip.

Every claim on this page maps to code you can read. Clone the repo, check out a tag, and build the exact binary we ship. Reproducible by design.

rVPN is free and open under AGPLv3, and always will be. Development is fully funded by PDG Global Limited; sales of the iOS and Android apps, together with donations, contribute towards development costs. The code never closes.

One protocol, every device. Native apps for phone and desktop, a command-line client for your servers, and the source code to port it anywhere we have not yet.

Free, open source, and ready on every platform. The apps are on the stores and the source is on GitHub today.

items.title: Apple has new Mac app coming to make running local AI models easy
items.summary: Article URL: https://9to5mac.com/2026/11/10/apple-has-new-mac-app-coming-to-make-running-local-ai-models-easy/ Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50446520 Points: 89 # Comments: 48
items.content:
Leaker Aaron Perris has discovered evidence of a new Mac app in the works at Apple called Harbor, which makes it easy to run local AI models across one or more Macs.

The Mac has been getting a lot more popular this year, both because of budget-friendly options like MacBook Neo but also as a tool for running AI models locally on Mac Studio, Mac mini, and more.

It seems Apple plans to lean harder into the latter use case, as leaker Aaron Perris has discovered a new Mac app called Harbor that’s been designed to turn your Mac into a private AI inference server.

Harbor turns your Mac into a private AI inference server. Run open-weight models locally on Apple silicon—your data never leaves your hardware, and nothing reaches the cloud. Connect multiple Mac computers over Thunderbolt 5 to pool unified memory, enabling large models and higher concurrency that a single computer can handle alone.

Harbor is currently in a private preview under Apple’s Claris brand, but it seems likely that we’ll see it launch to the public in the weeks and months ahead.

Are you interested in using Harbor on your Mac? Let us know in the comments.

items.title: First day of Ukraine peace talks constructive, Zelensky says
items.summary: Delegations from Kyiv, Washington and Moscow are in the United Arab Emirates for the first trilateral talks since February.
items.content:
The first of two days of trilateral talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US aimed at ending the war in Ukraine has concluded in Abu Dhabi.

While senior officials from Kyiv and Moscow were tight-lipped after the four hour-long discussions, President Volodymyr Zelensky, who was not at the talks, said they had proved "constructive and quite substantive".

Speaking from Paris, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio also said the meeting had been "very productive".

Although expectations for a breakthrough that ends Russia's full-scale war on Ukraine are low, US officials said earlier that Moscow and Kyiv were privately showing "a little bit of flexibility" on the issue of who would control Ukraine's eastern regions in a postwar scenario.

Zelensky also said that humanitarian issues such as prisoner of war exchanges had been discussed.

At the start of Tuesday's talks President Donald Trump's son-in-law, Jared Kushner, told delegates that the US had "narrowed the gaps" between the two sides, without providing details, and hoped to move towards a "solution that hopefully ends the war".

Kushner had said earlier the talks would be focused on addressing the "postwar security concerns" of both Russia and Ukraine.

Asked later at a news conference in Copenhagen about the approach of US officials to negotiations, Zelensky said: "I see changes. I'm very happy with what I hear."

Kushner and Trump peace envoy Steve Witkoff also met Ukrainian and European and Nato officials on the sidelines of the main meeting.

Until now European leaders have largely been excluded from peace talks, but they have pushed to be included in the discussions amid concerns that decisions about their continent's security would be made without them.

The Americans appear to support this, with Rubio acknowledging during a visit to Paris that the Europeans "are a part of solving this problem for the long term".

However, "the Russians have a bad taste in their mouth with the Europeans", according to a US official.

Some proposals favoured by EU officials - such as calling an unconditional ceasefire as a prerequisite for peace negotiations - are routinely rejected by Moscow. Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said on Tuesday that a truce would just allow Kyiv to regroup. "We will not agree to it," he said.

Moscow and Kyiv's positions are still far apart on ending the conflict.

A key area of disagreement involves Ukraine's eastern region of Donetsk, which is mostly occupied by Russia.

Moscow has demanded that Ukraine relinquish the parts of Donetsk it still holds, while Kyiv wants to freeze the contact line to maintain control over those areas, which it says are crucial to its future security.

While neither side has budged on these demands, the US official speaking on the eve of the talks suggested that this was just the public stance and that Moscow and Kyiv had shown "a little bit of flexibility, privately".

However, he acknowledged the issue would not be solved without discussions about a new "security architecture".

"They will not solve the Donetsk issue and the territorial issue until they know what the security architecture is going to be after the war," the official said. "And keep in mind, we're not going to be able to finalise one without the other."

For Ukraine, a post-war "security architecture" may include reassurance that allies will come to its aid if it comes under attack again. For Russia, that could be its longstanding ambition to see Nato roll back from Eastern Europe – which would be alarming to Europeans.

The framework being proposed includes security consultations and crisis communications hotlines, as well as "reciprocal de-escalation measures" between the two. The officials also floated the re-activation of the Nato-Russia Council that has been largely paused since 2022.

The last round of trilateral talks, held in Geneva in February, ended without a breakthrough. Soon after, the US-Israel war on Iran diverted Washington's attention from Ukraine, and no other discussions were held since.

From the start of his second term in office, US President Donald Trump – who once boasted he could end the war in Ukraine within a day – has spearheaded several rounds of talks to end the conflict, albeit with little success.

Meanwhile, his increasingly conciliatory approach towards Moscow has fuelled deep unease in Kyiv and across the European Union.

After meeting Kremlin envoy Kirill Dmitriev in Washington last week, Trump touted a forthcoming "big, beautiful agreement" on Ukraine that "might involve all of Europe".

Many in Ukraine are sceptical that this would result in a fair peace.

Ukrainian MP Oleksandr Merezhko, head of the foreign affairs parliamentary committee, told the BBC he believed Trump wanted "a quick deal at the expense of Ukraine", which will certainly be rejected by Kyiv.

The only way to make Russia's Vladimir Putin start real negotiations was by putting greater pressure on Russia through sanctions and deep strikes, Merezhko said.

"While Putin has a war machine up and running, he has no incentives to negotiate." He also mentioned recent moves by Trump, such as his deal to buy diesel from Russia, as something that "only encourages Moscow to continue the war".

Moscow's delegation in Abu Dhabi includes Kremlin aide Vladimir Medinsky, deputy foreign ministers Sergei Ryabkov and Mikhail Galuzin, spy chief Igor Kostyukov and army general Yury Zhigarlovsky.

Kyiv has sent several senior officials who have been part of previous negotiating teams, including Foreign Intelligence Service head Rustem Umerov, Volodymyr Zelensky's chief of staff Kyrylo Budanov, and MP Davyd Arakhamiya.

Away from Abu Dhabi, Russia continues to pummel Ukraine with deadly bombardments and strikes on energy infrastructure, viewed in Kyiv as proof that Moscow wants to corner Ukraine into accepting a deal on Russia's terms.

On Monday, Kushner was cautious to point out that the Abu Dhabi talks could at most "build momentum toward the next phase of negotiations".

"This is an extraordinarily difficult and complicated conflict," he wrote on X, adding the US was "approaching these discussions with determination and realism."
